content: The World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Bank Disease Control Priorities Third Edition (DCP3) have identified Voluntary Medical Male Circumcision (VMMC) as one of 44 essential surgical procedures. This designation is based on its ability to address significant health needs, its cost-effectiveness, and its feasibility for implementation. Evidence from 10 studies, including those conducted in Rwanda, South Africa, Uganda, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Tanzania, Kenya, and other sub-Saharan African regions, supports the cost-effectiveness of VMMC in reducing HIV incidence. A study in Tanzania demonstrated that a demand strategy intervention for VMMC resulted in lower costs per HIV infection averted (HIA) compared to standard care. For example, in Njombe, the cost per HIA was USD $1,424 versus $1,917, and in Tabora, it was USD $2,212 versus $3,018. Another study found that VMMC remained cost-effective even at a higher cost of USD $69 per circumcision, with cost-effectiveness estimates in Lesotho and Swaziland reported at USD $292 and USD $176 per HIA, respectively. The DMPPT (Decision Makers’ Program Planning Tool) model version 2 was applied in countries such as Malawi, South Africa, Swaziland, Uganda, and Tanzania. It projected the impact and costs of scaling up circumcision coverage from pre-intervention levels to 80% over a five-year period (2014–2018) and assessed outcomes over a 15-year horizon. The results were broadly consistent across these countries, with the lowest numbers of circumcisions per HIA observed in the 20–24, 25–29, and 30–34 age groups. However, circumcisions performed in younger age groups (e.g., 10–14 years) were projected to have a greater long-term impact. An updated analysis using the DMPPT 2 model estimated the impact of circumcisions performed by the end of 2014 across 14 priority countries in East and Southern Africa. If 80% coverage had been achieved by 2015 and maintained through 2025, the model projected significant reductions in HIV incidence. The age group 10–19 years accounted for 66% of circumcisions performed by 2014 and was projected to contribute 52% of the total HIAs by 2025. The median cost per HIA was estimated at USD $4,400, which compared favorably to other HIV prevention interventions. In South Africa, the greatest reduction in annual HIV risk was observed for circumcisions performed at age 25, corresponding to the peak age of HIV incidence. Circumcisions performed at younger ages (e.g., 0 or 10 years) showed delayed benefits, while those performed at older ages had proportionally lower indirect effects due to reduced secondary and higher-order HIV transmissions. Between four and five circumcisions were required to prevent one HIV infection for procedures performed at ages 0, 10, 15, and 20 years, but this number increased significantly for older age groups. The ASM (Age-Structured Model) applied to Zambia and Zimbabwe showed that while circumcising older men initially had the most immediate impact, circumcising younger men (under 30 years) over a 15-year period resulted in greater absolute reductions in HIV incidence, fewer circumcisions per infection averted, and lower costs per infection averted. Scaling up to 80% circumcision coverage in specific five-year age strata over seven years (2011–2017) and maintaining it through 2050 was projected to be cost-effective, with the lowest cost per HIV infection averted observed in the 15–24 age group. In the context of expanding antiretroviral therapy (ART) to meet the UNAIDS 90–90–90 treatment targets by 2020, scaling up VMMC in countries such as Lesotho, Malawi, South Africa, and Uganda was projected to further reduce HIV incidence. While this required additional short-term costs, total annual costs were projected to decrease from 2020 onward. Adolescent VMMC was found to be highly cost-effective in base-case scenarios, though this cost-effectiveness was sensitive to changes in input variables. Adult VMMC, however, was neither cost-saving nor highly cost-effective when considering only the direct benefits to the circumcised individual. Equity considerations revealed that traditional community values significantly influence the acceptability of VMMC, thereby impacting health equity. For example, in rural Malawi, individuals from ethnic groups other than the Yao, as well as Yaos in the central region, were more likely to be disadvantaged due to negative attitudes toward VMMC. In urban South Africa, no significant health inequities were observed across socio-demographic characteristics. However, in urban China, male injection drug users of Han ethnicity were disadvantaged due to beliefs that VMMC would not be effective, would reduce sexual ability, and would be prohibitively expensive. Feasibility studies conducted in India, Zambia, Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, the Dominican Republic, and sub-Saharan Africa identified barriers to VMMC implementation, including transportation challenges, lack of peer support, limited knowledge about VMMC’s protective effects against HIV, and fear of the procedure’s irreversibility. Facilitators included community support and education. Some studies noted limitations, such as self-reported data being subject to social desirability bias and sampling methodologies that may not be generalizable. In summary, VMMC is a cost-effective intervention for HIV prevention, particularly when targeted at younger age groups. However, its implementation requires addressing barriers related to equity, community acceptance, and logistical challenges. Further research is needed to understand its cost-effectiveness in diverse cultural and economic settings.
